dossiers.label: The soul as self-mover
dossiers.about: Every soul is immortal: what moves itself never ceases to move, and is the source and beginning of motion for all else; a beginning cannot come to be or perish.

passage.end_quote: περὶ μὲν οὖν ἀθανασίας αὐτῆς ἱκανῶς

parts.label: Every soul is immortal
Only the self-moving never ceases to move
parts.quote: μόνον δὴ τὸ αὑτὸ κινοῦν, ἅτε οὐκ ἀπολεῖπον ἑαυτό, οὔποτε λήγει κινούμενον

parts.label: The source and beginning of motion
So the soul is unborn and immortal
parts.quote: ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἀγένητόν τε καὶ ἀθάνατον ψυχὴ ἂν εἴη

echoes.quote: τὴν δυναμένην αὐτὴν αὑτὴν κινεῖν κίνησιν
echoes.why: Laws X defines soul as the motion able to move itself, and makes it prior to body.

related.why: From the soul's immortality Socrates turns to its form, the charioteer.

evidence.quote: περὶ δὲ τῆς ἰδέας αὐτῆς ὧδε λεκτέον

web.title: Phaedrus (dialogue)
web.quote: A soul is always in motion and as a self-mover has no beginning

dossiers.label: The charioteer and the winged horses
dossiers.about: The soul is like a winged pair of horses and their charioteer. The gods' horses are good; ours are mixed. Following the gods round the heavens, souls glimpse the place beyond the heavens, fall, and regrow their wings through love of beauty.

passage.start_quote: ἐοικέτω δὴ συμφύτῳ δυνάμει ὑποπτέρου ζεύγους τε καὶ ἡνιόχου

parts.label: A winged pair and a charioteer
Zeus drives his winged chariot, the gods follow
parts.quote: ὁ μὲν δὴ μέγας ἡγεμὼν ἐν οὐρανῷ Ζεύς, ἐλαύνων πτηνὸν ἅρμα

parts.label: The place beyond the heavens
Being that truly is, seen by intellect alone
The plain of truth
The ordinance of Adrasteia
Learning as recollection of what the soul once saw
parts.quote: τοῦτο δʼ ἐστὶν ἀνάμνησις ἐκείνων ἅ ποτʼ εἶδεν ἡμῶν ἡ ψυχὴ

parts.label: The two horses described
parts.quote: τῶν δὲ δὴ ἵππων ὁ μέν, φαμέν, ἀγαθός, ὁ δʼ οὔ

parts.label: Lovers who win grow wings together

diagram.title: The two horses, 253d–e
diagram.about: Socrates' description of the two horses, word by word.

columns.head: The good horse
columns.quote: ὁ μὲν τοίνυν αὐτοῖν ἐν τῇ καλλίονι στάσει ὢν

cells.quote: τό τε εἶδος ὀρθὸς καὶ διηρθρωμένος

cells.text: lover of honour with temperance and modesty
cells.quote: τιμῆς ἐραστὴς μετὰ σωφροσύνης τε καὶ αἰδοῦς

cells.text: by command and word alone, no whip
shaggy-eared, deaf, barely yields to whip and goad

echoes.why: The Timaeus: the maker sets each soul in a star 'as in a chariot'.
The Republic's three parts of the soul, which the charioteer and two horses are often read as.

related.why: The myth follows the proof of the soul's immortality.

evidence.quote: περὶ δὲ τῆς ἰδέας αὐτῆς ὧδε λεκτέον

related.why: The soul divided in three here too, two horse-shaped and the charioteer.

testimonia.says: Proclus reads the Timaeus's 'vehicle' of the soul with the Phaedrus's charioteer.

by.jowett: heaven which is above the heavens

web.title: Phaedrus (dialogue)
web.quote: A soul, says Socrates, is like the "natural union of a team of winged horses and their charioteer"

web.title: Plato's Myths
web.quote: the myth of the winged soul (Phaedrus 246a–249d)

dossiers.label: Divine madness
dossiers.about: The greatest goods come to us through madness given by the gods: prophecy, the purifying madness of rites, the madness of the Muses, and the fourth and best, the lover's.

passage.end_quote: παρὰ θεῶν ἡ τοιαύτη μανία δίδοται

parts.label: The greatest goods come through madness
parts.quote: τὰ μέγιστα τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἡμῖν γίγνεται διὰ μανίας, θείᾳ μέντοι δόσει διδομένης

parts.label: Prophecy: the priestess at Delphi
parts.quote: ἥ τε γὰρ δὴ ἐν Δελφοῖς προφῆτις

parts.label: Love's madness, given by the gods
parts.quote: παρὰ θεῶν ἡ τοιαύτη μανία δίδοται

echoes.why: Socrates later sums up the four kinds and their gods: Apollo, Dionysus, the Muses, Aphrodite and Eros.
The Ion: the poet is a light and winged and holy thing, out of his mind when inspired.

dossiers.label: The cicadas
dossiers.about: The cicadas singing overhead in the noon heat were once men who forgot to eat for joy of the Muses' song; they report to the Muses who honours them, and to Calliope and Urania those who live in philosophy.

parts.label: The cicadas singing overhead in the heat
parts.quote: ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς ἡμῶν οἱ τέττιγες ᾁδοντες

parts.label: Calliope and Urania honour those who live in philosophy
parts.quote: τῇ δὲ πρεσβυτάτῃ Καλλιόπῃ καὶ τῇ μετʼ αὐτὴν Οὐρανίᾳ τοὺς ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ διάγοντάς

parts.label: So we must talk, and not sleep at noon

echoes.why: At the opening the shrill summer song of the cicada chorus answers the setting by the Ilissus.

dossiers.label: Theuth and the invention of writing
dossiers.about: Theuth offers King Thamus writing as a drug for memory; Thamus answers it is a drug for reminding, and will give the appearance of wisdom, not wisdom. Written words cannot answer or defend themselves; the living word written in the soul is their legitimate brother.

passage.start_quote: ἤκουσα τοίνυν περὶ Ναύκρατιν τῆς Αἰγύπτου
passage.end_quote: οὗ ὁ γεγραμμένος εἴδωλον ἄν τι λέγοιτο δικαίως

parts.label: Theuth of Naucratis, inventor of number and letters
parts.quote: αὐτῷ δὲ ὄνομα τῷ δαίμονι εἶναι Θεύθ

parts.label: Writing as a drug of memory and wisdom
Thamus: forgetfulness in the soul, a drug for reminding
The appearance of wisdom, not its truth
A written word always needs its father's help
The living word, its legitimate brother

echoes.quote: ῥητὸν γὰρ οὐδαμῶς ἐστιν ὡς ἄλλα μαθήματα
echoes.why: The Seventh Letter: there is no writing of Plato's on these matters, for it cannot be put into words like other learning.

related.why: The Seventh Letter's distrust of writing.

evidence.quote: ῥητὸν γὰρ οὐδαμῶς ἐστιν ὡς ἄλλα μαθήματα

web.title: Phaedrus (dialogue)
web.quote: commenting on the gift of writing from the Egyptian god Theuth to King Thamus

dossiers.label: Collection and division
dossiers.about: Two procedures: to see scattered things together under one form, and to cut them again by forms 'at the joints, as nature grew them', not hacking like a bad butcher. Socrates is a lover of them and calls those who can do it dialecticians.

parts.label: To bring the scattered into one form
parts.quote: εἰς μίαν τε ἰδέαν συνορῶντα ἄγειν τὰ πολλαχῇ διεσπαρμένα

parts.label: To cut at the joints, not like a bad butcher
parts.quote: κατʼ ἄρθρα ᾗ πέφυκεν, καὶ μὴ ἐπιχειρεῖν καταγνύναι μέρος μηδέν, κακοῦ μαγείρου τρόπῳ χρώμενον

parts.label: A lover of divisions and collections
Those who can do this, 'dialecticians'

echoes.why: The Sophist: dividing by kinds is the dialectical science.
The Statesman: divide limb by limb, like a sacrificial victim.

related.why: The Sophist's angler is the method shown at work.

dossiers.label: Boreas and Oreithyia: know thyself
dossiers.about: By the Ilissus Phaedrus asks whether Socrates believes the tale of Boreas snatching Oreithyia. Socrates has no leisure to rationalise myths: he does not yet know himself, as the Delphic inscription bids, whether he is a beast more complex than Typhon or a gentler, simpler creature.

passage.start_quote: οὐκ ἐνθένδε μέντοι ποθὲν ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰλισο
passage.end_quote: θείας τινὸς καὶ ἀτύφου μοίρας φύσει μετέχον

parts.label: Is this where Boreas carried off Oreithyia?
Know thyself, as the Delphic inscription says
Not these, but myself: Typhon or a gentler creature?

echoes.why: The First Alcibiades turns on the same inscription.
The Charmides: Critias reads the inscription as a greeting of the god.

dossiers.label: The prayer to Pan
dossiers.about: Socrates' prayer at the end of the Phaedrus: to be beautiful within, the outer to be friendly to the inner, to count the wise man rich, and to have only as much gold as a temperate man can carry.

passage.start_quote: ὦ φίλε Πάν τε καὶ ἄλλοι ὅσοι τῇδε θεοί
passage.end_quote: κοινὰ γὰρ τὰ τῶν φίλων. ἴωμεν

parts.label: Beautiful within
The wise man rich
Friends have all things in common

echoes.why: The proverb returns in the Republic, of the guardians' common life.
